query: How can Singapore Airlines improve its overall rating and recommendation rate, especially on flights where passengers do not recommend it (Recommended = no)?

per_column.name: cabin_crew_attitude
per_column.rationale: A candidate cause of the rating/recommendation. Crew attitude plausibly drives passenger satisfaction, so it is a treatment/driver being attributed, not a common cause of another treatment.

per_column.name: service_proactivity
per_column.rationale: Another service-quality lever whose effect on the outcome is being attributed. It is a parallel driver of the rating, not a common cause of both a treatment and the outcome.

per_column.name: ground_service_quality
per_column.rationale: Check-in/boarding/connection problems are candidate causes of a poor rating; a driver/treatment, not an adjustment-set confounder.

per_column.name: ife_quality
per_column.rationale: In-flight entertainment quality is a candidate cause of satisfaction. Treatment/driver of the outcome.

per_column.name: disruption_handling_quality
per_column.rationale: How disruptions are handled directly drives whether passengers recommend; a candidate cause, not a confounder of another cause.

per_column.name: complaint_resolution_outcome
per_column.rationale: Resolution outcome is a candidate cause of the recommendation decision. It sits on a driver path to the outcome, not a common cause of both a treatment and outcome.

per_column.name: digital_system_failure
per_column.rationale: A binary operational failure flag treated as a candidate cause of dissatisfaction; a driver/treatment.

per_column.name: value_for_money_perception
per_column.rationale: This nearly duplicates the existing 'Value For Money' rating dimension and is an evaluative judgement that lies ON the path from service quality to overall rating/recommendation; adjusting for it would be a mediator error, not a confounder.

per_column.name: service_decline_perceived
per_column.rationale: A summary perception (actual service quality -> perceived decline -> lower rating). It sits on the causal path and is close to the outcome, so it is a mediator rather than a common-cause confounder.

per_column.name: cabin_class_product_gap
per_column.rationale: The gap between product and class expectations is an evaluative judgement directly upstream of (and nearly equivalent to) satisfaction; it is on the treatment->outcome path, i.e., a mediator, not a confounder.

per_column.name: flight_duration_category
per_column.rationale: A genuine contextual/pre-treatment variable derived from Route: flight length plausibly shapes the level and salience of service delivered (meals, IFE use, crew interaction) AND shapes expectations/ratings, so it can bias attribution if not adjusted. This is the only column functioning as a common-cause confounder, though it is closer to an effect modifier.

judge.rationale: The added columns richly supply the TREATMENT side of a causal attribution: they decompose the outcome into many candidate service-quality causes (crew attitude, proactivity, ground service, IFE, disruption/complaint handling, digital failures). However, the set is essentially a DRIVER DECOMPOSITION, not a confounder-adjusted causal design. Several columns (value_for_money_perception, service_decline_perceived, cabin_class_product_gap) are evaluative perceptions that lie ON the path to the rating — mediators/near-outcomes whose adjustment would bias, not clarify, attribution. Crucially, the operator surfaced almost no genuine CONFOUNDERS — variables that jointly cause a treatment AND the outcome and must be adjusted for. The one contextual variable, flight_duration_category, is not named in the query and is the only plausible common-cause/effect-modifier, and even it is borderline. Traveller type, class, and route (natural confounders) exist only in the original schema, not among the added columns. Thus the specific causal-attribution claim is only weakly met: treatment present = yes, but the confounder (adjustment) side is largely missing, so confounder_quality is low.
